# Completion and checkpoints

## Task commit contract

One executable task closes in one task-owned commit. Cumulative multi-task closing commits are forbidden. The closing commit's tree must contain that task's verified result and applicable tests/documentation; its task-owned diff includes the remaining result changes, required current completion evidence or its established link, and the initial unchecked-to-checked transition in owning TASKS or FEATURE-TASKS. The authorized partial-checkpoint condition below governs result portions already committed. Never commit the task result first and defer its completion checkbox to a separate `mark complete` commit. Complete, commit, inspect and publish this boundary before starting another task.

- Use exactly one owning task ID at the beginning of the subject under **sdd-report**'s [task subject rules](../../sdd-report/references/object-drafts.md#task-commit-subjects). A conforming subject cannot make bundled or split closing contents compliant.
- Apply the same contract to code, tests, documentation and explicit milestone/phase review/report tasks. For a review task, the substantive review/report and acceptance evidence are the task result; a subject saying “Complete review” without that result does not close it.
- Do not include another executable task's result or initial completion checkbox. Shared files are allowed only when their staged hunks belong to this task or required scoped bootstrap; inspect ownership rather than grouping tasks for convenience. Several verified issue references for one task are not multiple task ownership.
- Eligible milestone/phase parent checkboxes may accompany the final task without counting as extra executable task closure. A justified later parent-only status/evidence follow-up identifies its single owning review/final task and boundary; this exception never permits deferred initial task checkboxes or bundled task results.
- Explicitly authorized partial checkpoints retain the task unchecked and describe incomplete work. Later scoped task-specific repairs retain their actual identity and evidence, without claiming another initial closure. These cases mean one closing commit per task, not exactly one commit ever associated with a task. Non-task campaign, preparation and merge work must not invent task IDs.

When explicitly authorized partial checkpoints already contain some or all production edits for the task result, the closing commit finishes the remaining task-owned work, includes the initial completion checkbox and current evidence, and identifies those checkpoints in that evidence. Inspect the complete resulting task state as well as the closing diff; do not duplicate unchanged code merely to create a production diff. Never relabel an ordinary result-first/checkbox-later violation as an authorized partial checkpoint after the fact.

Before committing, inspect the intended subject and actual staged result, checklist delta and evidence. Identify the one closing task and confirm its exact owning entry and initial completion transition; distinguish parent status from executable task status. Exclude unrelated staged content and another task's hunks while preserving them. If ownership or separation is unsafe, block the commit rather than bundle work. After committing, inspect the actual subject and committed diff against its parent for the same facts, plus remaining staged/unstaged changes, before publishing and advancing. Do not infer compliance from the draft, checkbox, filename or subject alone.

### Task persistence audit and recovery

On continuation, inspect the latest claimed closing boundary and any pending result/status for the selected work. Before integration, audit the task closing commits for the selected completed range through relevant merge parents: each exact owning task ID has its own closing commit establishing the verified complete result, current evidence and initial completion transition together, with referenced authorized partial checkpoints inspected when applicable, without another task's result/closure, and its subject satisfies the task rules. Account separately for authorized partial checkpoints, repairs and parent-only follow-ups. Merge summaries do not substitute for these commits. Keep the audit bounded to the active selected work and established baseline; do not reopen unrelated closed campaigns or require a new registry, hook or journal.

If malformed subjects, bundled results, split result/status or uncertain ownership already exist, preserve history and valid work. Report the affected task IDs, commits, inspected diffs/evidence and publication state; block affected advancement/integration until the manager resolves an authorized scoped recovery or explicit exception. A published violation does not authorize rebase, reset, force-push, task replay or retrospective issue reconstruction. A forward status/evidence correction may reconcile current truth when authorized, but does not make the original history compliant. Do not disguise a split closing commit as a permitted parent-only follow-up or claim that changing a subject repairs composition.

Also stop for an unresolved implementation or push blocker or the user's pause instruction.
- Report implemented capabilities, completed IDs, acceptance and exit-condition evidence, unresolved failures or limitations, commit and push state, pending issue reconciliation, and remaining tasks. Distinguish task/working-branch completion from integration into the established target and its remote publication.

Use **sdd-manage**'s **Git workflows** reference after the selected tasks and applicable exits are verified, committed, and pushed. Task persistence remains per task. For a feature/revision, integrate only its coherent authorized boundary. Verify the entire prospective branch difference before integrating: an existing branch containing unrelated or unfinished work is a scope conflict. A pause or blocker returns branch state without a partial merge.

An explicit selected document set governs incorporation. A narrow task/range request does not authorize incorporation of all feature documents or integration of unfinished work: merge only when the selected branch difference and documents are coherent within that scope; otherwise report the unmet prerequisite. Retain active sources and pending reassessment until their established requirements are satisfied.

When the applicable integration gate is met, verify working-branch acceptance, then merge with an explicit two-parent commit, verify the merged state, and push the target. **sdd-manage** coordinates this Git integration; a direct invocation follows the same protocol. Report task completion separately from branch acceptance, target integration, and published merge status. ## Scope and authority

TextStats provides predictable line and word counts through a silent Python API and module-entry CLI. The accepted [PROJECT](PROJECT.md), [ARCHITECTURE](ARCHITECTURE.md) and [DECOMPOSITION](DECOMPOSITION.md) govern product purpose and structural boundaries. Python 3.11+, standard-library runtime and unittest are required. No implementation exists.

R-001 through R-013 specify the intended initial two-phase system; milestone labels identify delivery obligations without authorizing implementation. F-001 through F-004 retain the later separately requested range feature's contract as a deferred compatibility constraint. That feature is outside the initial executable hierarchy. No focused specification children are needed.

## Public API and values

### R-001 Direct exports and statistics

Importable `textstats` directly exports `TextStats`, `count_text` and `count_file`. `TextStats(lines: int, words: int)` is immutable, with integer, nonnegative fields and value equality. Construction with a negative count raises ValueError; a non-integer count raises TypeError. Boolean values are excluded from the count domain despite Python's bool/int subtype relationship. Invalid construction cannot create a value with an invalid field. Exception wording is not prescribed. These construction details settle the design's previously delegated integer-domain boundary.

### R-002 Whole-input counting API

The signatures are `count_text(text: str, *, strip_bom: bool = True) -> TextStats` and `count_file(path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, strip_bom: bool = True) -> TextStats`. The keyword-only policy has the same meaning for both. Both return whole-input counts, are silent on stdout/stderr, and expose no range parameter. Valid text/file calls with identical decoded contents and policy return equal values. Behavior for arguments outside the annotated input domains is not otherwise prescribed.

### R-003 Line semantics

CRLF is one terminator; lone CR and lone LF are terminators. Each terminator contributes one line. A nonempty final unterminated segment contributes one line. Empty text contributes zero lines, and a trailing terminator creates no additional phantom line. Other Unicode separators, including U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029, do not terminate lines. Apply R-005 before deciding whether a final segment is nonempty.

### R-004 Word semantics

The word count equals the number of elements produced by Python `str.split()` with no separator argument on the counted text. Unicode whitespace separates words and runs of whitespace add no empty words. Word semantics do not broaden line-terminator semantics.

### R-005 BOM policy

With `strip_bom=True`, remove exactly one leading U+FEFF from the complete text. Preserve a second leading BOM and every interior BOM. With `strip_bom=False`, preserve all BOMs. Retained BOM is ordinary non-whitespace, including in otherwise empty content. CLI `--keep-bom` selects the retaining policy. No other text normalization or rewriting is permitted.

### R-006 Named-file decode, failure and ownership

Read complete input as bytes and decode strict UTF-8, retaining newline characters exactly. A named-file API call raises the applicable OSError subclass for missing/unreadable files or read failures and UnicodeDecodeError for invalid UTF-8. Do not return a partial result. Close every handle opened by the utility on success and failure. Inputs remain byte-for-byte unchanged. No fallback encoding, replacement character or locale-dependent decode is permitted.

## CLI contracts

### R-007 Baseline named-file invocation

Phase 1 milestone 1.1 supplies `python -m textstats [--keep-bom] INPUT` with exactly one named-file input. Support `--` to terminate option processing so dash-prefixed filenames are usable. A literal filename `-` is a named-file input before milestone 2.2; after stdin delivery it denotes stdin, and an actual file with that name can be addressed as `./-`. Recognized options can precede or follow the input, subject to `--` termination. Do not interpret options appearing after `--` as options.

Success returns status 0, stdout exactly `lines=<N> words=<N>\n` using nonnegative decimal integers, and empty stderr. This remains the default format in phase 2. Help through `-h` or `--help` returns 0 with useful usage/options on stdout and empty stderr; it requires no input acquisition. Help output's exact prose is unrestricted.

### R-008 CLI failures and usage

Phase 1 milestone 1.2 supplies complete failure handling. Missing/unreadable named files, input read failures and decode failures return status 1 with nonempty stderr identifying the input and cause, empty stdout and no traceback. Missing input, extra inputs and unknown options return status 2 with useful usage/error stderr, empty stdout and no traceback. Parse and validate invocation before acquiring input. Status categories are stable across the phase 2 options. No input is changed and no partial result appears on stdout.

### R-009 JSON output

Phase 2 milestone 2.1 supplies `--json`, composing with `--keep-bom` and named-file input. Success returns 0 with one JSON object and a final newline, empty stderr, and exactly the keys `lines` and `words`, each containing an integer equal to the text-format count. No extra fields or JSON booleans are permitted. Key order and spacing are unrestricted. Without `--json`, preserve R-007 text output. Failures retain R-008, regardless of output selection.

### R-010 Stdin input

Phase 2 milestone 2.2 supplies input token `-` as stdin. Read bytes until EOF and decode complete content as strict UTF-8 independently of locale, without closing stdin. Apply the same counting/BOM/output policies as named files. Empty stdin returns (0, 0). Read or decode failure returns 1, identifies stdin and the cause on stderr, and produces empty stdout with no traceback. Stdin acquisition does not alter `count_file` semantics or add an API export. Output succeeds only after complete input acquisition and decoding.

## Deferred range feature

### F-001 Range grammar and validation

A separately requested feature adds exactly one `--lines START:END` or `--lines=START:END`. START and END consist solely of ASCII decimal digits and represent positive inclusive one-based endpoints with START <= END. Leading zeros are decimal. No arbitrary endpoint or digit-count limit is permitted. Reject signs, surrounding or interior whitespace, Unicode digits, zero, reversal, open endpoints, extra colons, missing values and repeated range options. Repetition across the two spelling forms is also invalid. Reject with usage status 2, useful stderr, empty stdout and no traceback before acquiring input. Valid very large decimal endpoints must remain valid despite any interpreter conversion safeguard.

### F-002 Selection semantics and decode ordering

Decode the complete input before selecting lines; invalid bytes after END still fail under R-008. Apply R-005 exactly once to complete decoded input before numbering. Select inclusive one-based logical lines under R-003, preserving each selected segment's contents and terminators. If END exceeds EOF, select the available subset; if START exceeds EOF, select empty content. Count the selected content under R-003/R-004 without further BOM stripping. An interior BOM exposed at the beginning of selected text must remain ordinary non-whitespace.

### F-003 Composition and delivery boundary

Range selection composes with `--keep-bom` and `--json` in either option order, using either accepted range spelling. Preserve default text output and R-008 error categories. Named-file text/JSON range behavior is the feature's delivery boundary. The public API remains whole-input with no range parameter or new export. Source-independent selection must be compatible with future stdin, but this feature does not implement or pull forward stdin acquisition/delivery.

# TextStats architecture

## Scope and governing input

This document describes the intended architecture for the capabilities and staged scope in the accepted [project brief](PROJECT.md). No product implementation exists. The public surface is an importable `textstats` API and `python -m textstats`; counting has no runtime dependencies beyond Python 3.11+ and the standard library.

## Major blocks and dependency direction

| Block | Responsibility and dependencies |
| --- | --- |
| Counting core | Own immutable statistics and text semantics: BOM normalization, CRLF/CR/LF logical-line handling and Unicode whitespace word counting. It depends on Python strings and immutable results, with no filesystem, CLI or process-stream dependency. |
| Input acquisition | Own strict UTF-8 decoding and named-file handle lifetime. It supplies decoded text to the counting pipeline and propagates acquisition/decode errors. Future stdin acquisition uses bytes and retains external stream ownership. |
| Public API facade | Directly expose the three requested public exports. `count_text` invokes the text pipeline; `count_file` acquires named-file text and invokes equivalent whole-input counting. Both return statistics silently, retaining API exceptions. |
| CLI orchestration | Parse and validate the requested invocation before acquiring input, select BOM/output policies, invoke the counting pipeline and translate input failures into CLI diagnostics/status. It depends on acquisition and core contracts; neither depends on CLI. |
| Presentation | Format a completed result as the required text output or the later JSON object. The CLI owns stdout/stderr effects and process status; presentation contains no input acquisition or counting rules. |

These are logical responsibility blocks, not a requirement for separate files or classes. Detailed collaborating components belong in decomposition and physical allocation in layout. There is no dependency cycle or global mutable counting state. The API and CLI share counting and decoding semantics rather than maintaining independent algorithms.

## Text pipeline and ownership

Acquisition finishes strict decoding before a result can be computed or emitted. The text pipeline removes at most one leading BOM according to the selected policy, then operates on normalized text. Whole-input API calls never select a range. The pipeline provides a counting path for already normalized text so the later CLI range path cannot strip a newly exposed interior BOM.

A shared logical-line representation or traversal recognizes only CRLF, CR and LF and preserves terminators and content. Both counting and future selection must use this semantic boundary; Python's broader Unicode `splitlines` behavior is unsuitable. Word counting remains independent, using `str.split` semantics on the counted content. Decomposition will settle the small internal interfaces without adding public exports.

The future range pipeline is acquisition and complete decode, BOM normalization once, logical-line selection, then counting and presentation. Parsing/validation precedes acquisition. Selection does not depend on whether text originated from a file or stdin. This supports the requested compatibility constraint without implementing the range feature or moving stdin into its delivery scope.

Input acquisition owns handles it opens and closes them on success and failure. Callers retain ownership of supplied process streams, including future stdin. No block writes input content. Statistics are immutable values; transient decoded strings and selected content have invocation-local lifetime. The default architecture holds complete decoded input in memory, which simplifies strict complete-decode and no-partial-result guarantees. No bounded-memory target was requested; streaming remains a future reconsideration if a concrete input-size constraint arises.

## Failure and output boundaries

API adapters allow the required filesystem and decode exception types to reach callers and produce no output. CLI orchestration distinguishes usage failures from input/read/decode failures and maps them to the prescribed statuses. Successful acquisition and counting must complete before stdout emission; diagnostics identify the affected input, and expected user failures do not expose a traceback. Presentation receives a complete immutable result, preventing partial count output during read/decode failure.

The CLI selects text output by default; JSON is a later output policy over the same statistics. Byte acquisition for future stdin keeps strict UTF-8 decoding independent of locale. Option parsing is a CLI concern and does not alter public whole-input API signatures.

## Consequential choices and verification seams

Use plain functions and a small immutable result value. Separate pure text processing from I/O and process effects because they have different failure/lifetime rules and verification seams. A monolithic CLI would couple reusable API behavior to streams; a class hierarchy, plugin system or configurable decoding layer would introduce unsupported variation. The selected function pipeline provides the required extension seams with less state and indirection.

Unit tests can exercise immutable results, BOM policy and logical-line/word semantics directly. Integration tests can exercise named-file acquisition, subprocess CLI output/status, later JSON/stdin behavior and extracted-source module execution. Product suites remain nonempty and discoverable under the requested unit/integration directories; coordinator workflow fixtures stay separately owned. API/module documentation and README usage will expose the same contracts used by these checks.

The distribution boundary is a source package that remains importable and supports module execution after extraction. Package contents and the executable verification command are planning/layout decisions. No additional runtime dependency, installed console-script entry or network service is required.

## Review and next stage

Owner review checked responsibility ownership, acyclic dependency direction, strict UTF-8 and handle lifetime, no-partial-result boundaries, BOM normalization exactly once, shared terminator semantics and source-independent future selection against the accepted PROJECT. No unresolved architectural decision blocks decomposition. No focused children are needed for this compact system, and no code or performance test has been run for the proposed arrangement.

Assessment checked the complete document against PROJECT and the product request and found no material issue; coordinator evidence is `deeffb6`. This scoped decision authorizes decomposition and does not preaccept later documents or implementation.
# TextStats component decomposition

## Governing design and scope

This component model refines the accepted [architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md) and [project brief](PROJECT.md). Components are logical units with stable design identities; internal function names below express interface shape and may be finalized during implementation without changing their obligations. They prescribe no physical file inventory or implementation order. No production code exists.

## Components and boundaries

| ID / component | Provided boundary and owner responsibility | Required collaborators and exclusions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C-001 Statistics value | Public immutable `TextStats(lines: int, words: int)` with nonnegative counts. Own construction invariants and value representation. | No acquisition, output or normalization. SPEC will settle invalid-construction exceptions and integer-domain details. |
| C-002 BOM normalization | Internal `normalize_text(text, strip_bom) -> str`; remove exactly one leading BOM when selected and retain all other characters. Own this policy once per pipeline invocation. | Strings only; no decode, line selection or counting. |
| C-003 Logical-line traversal | Internal `logical_lines(normalized_text)` yields nonempty logical segments with their original content and CRLF/CR/LF terminators; blank terminated lines remain segments. A final nonempty unterminated segment is yielded; empty text yields none. | No BOM handling or Unicode-whitespace splitting. This is the shared line boundary for counting and future selection. |
| C-004 Normalized counting | Internal `count_normalized(normalized_text) -> TextStats`; derive line count from C-003 and word count from `str.split` on the same text. | C-001 and C-003; never normalize again, acquire input or emit output. |
| C-005 Byte acquisition and decode | Acquire complete bytes from a named file and decode strict UTF-8 without text newline translation. Own opening and closing named-file handles on every path. Future borrowed-stdin acquisition reads its binary stream to EOF and never closes it. | Python filesystem/binary stream operations; no BOM removal, range selection, counting or output. Preserve acquisition and decode exceptions for callers. |
| C-006 Public API adapters | Directly expose C-001 plus `count_text(text: str, *, strip_bom: bool = True)` and `count_file(path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, strip_bom: bool = True)`. Adapt whole-input requests to C-002/C-004; file calls use C-005 first. | No CLI invocation or range argument; no extra public export, stream output or exception-to-status translation. |
| C-007 CLI invocation parser | Validate option syntax and exactly one input; provide input identity and BOM/output policy. Future range validation supplies numeric endpoints before input acquisition. | No C-005 access during parsing. Help and usage termination belong to CLI control, not API behavior. |
| C-008 CLI controller | Coordinate parsed invocation, acquisition, text pipeline and result rendering; map expected usage/acquisition/decode failures to identifying diagnostics/status. Own process-stream writes. | C-007, C-005, C-002, C-004 and C-009; no separate counting algorithm. Future C-010 sits between normalization and counting. |
| C-009 Result rendering | Internal renderer transforms completed C-001 into the specified text string or later JSON object plus newline. | No stream write, acquisition, normalization or counting. Controller chooses format and emits result. |
| C-010 Future range selection | Future internal `select_lines(normalized_text, start, end) -> str`, with inclusive one-based endpoints, preserving available selected segments and their terminators. | C-003 and validated CLI endpoints; no input-source dependency or BOM normalization. This future feature is outside the initial two-phase executable hierarchy. |

The identities group coherent verification obligations and provide downstream specification/planning traceability; they do not require one module or task per row. No focused children are necessary for this compact component set.

## Collaboration and data lifetime

`count_text` receives the complete string, normalizes through C-002 and counts through C-004. `count_file` uses C-005 to acquire/decode complete input, then follows the equivalent public whole-input pipeline. The API adapters return C-001 without writing stdout/stderr. Strict byte decoding preserves CRLF, lone CR and LF exactly rather than relying on universal-newline text mode.

The CLI parses and validates before C-005 acquires input. C-008 then normalizes exactly once and passes normalized text to C-004. Only a completed value reaches C-009 and only the controller writes its output. If the future range feature is separately requested, C-008 passes normalized text through C-010 first and sends its result directly to C-004, bypassing C-002 a second time. Consequently, a BOM exposed inside selected content remains ordinary non-whitespace.

C-003 yields segments such as `a\r\n`, `b c\r` and `d\n` without changing characters. Selecting whole segments and concatenating them preserves line boundaries for C-004 and preserves Unicode whitespace for word counting. Segment enumeration can be lazy over the already decoded string; it does not imply streaming decode or partial input acceptance. Counting and range selection share the same terminator semantics.

For future stdin, C-005 obtains bytes from the externally owned binary input stream and returns decoded text after EOF; the remainder of the pipeline is identical. The parser/controller activate that acquisition choice only at its delivery milestone. Decoded strings, segments and results are local to an invocation; there is no shared mutable counting state or input mutation.

## Failure and verification seams

C-001 can be checked through construction, immutability and value assertions. C-002 can be checked with empty, BOM-only, repeated-leading and interior-BOM strings under both policies. C-003/C-004 can be checked with mixed terminators, consecutive blank lines, final segments and Unicode whitespace/separators. These seams need no filesystem or subprocess.

C-005 can be checked with temporary valid/invalid UTF-8 files, missing/unreadable paths and controlled read failures, including handle cleanup. Borrowed-stream checks later verify byte decoding, locale independence, EOF and retained ownership. C-006 checks establish direct imports, whole-input equivalence, silence and exception propagation. No partial decoded/count result is returned on input failure.

C-007 checks establish help/usage behavior and, later, range validation before acquisition, including repeated options and unbounded decimal endpoints. C-008/C-009 checks establish exact text output, JSON field/type constraints, empty failure stdout and identifying stderr/status. Subprocess integration validates the real module entry and extracted-source distribution; component-level seams support controlled acquisition failures that can be difficult to reproduce reliably through platform permissions.

C-010's future checks cover available subsets, beyond-EOF emptiness, blank selected lines, mixed terminators, bad bytes after END and interior BOM exposure. These are deferred feature obligations, not tests or delivery included in this preparation request.

## Contract handoff and review

The product request already fixes line/word/BOM semantics, API signatures, output and exit categories. SPEC will provide the full objective acceptance matrix, exact staged CLI grammar, invalid constructor/input-type contracts where required, useful diagnostic expectations and the public documentation/distribution obligations. Internal naming is provisional; public exports are fixed. There is no unresolved component decision that requires upstream architecture revision.

# Test-first cycle

Use the cycle for one observable behavior at a time. Read [writing good tests](writing-good-tests.md) before writing or changing a test. Run the project's actual commands; commands in examples are not evidence from the current task.

## RED

1. State the contract and the defect the test should catch. Write a focused test with an independently established expected result.
2. Execute the test before the relevant production change. Inspect the failure and confirm it demonstrates the missing or incorrect behavior.
3. Distinguish a behavioral failure from collection, import, syntax, dependency, or environment failures. Fix test setup or report the blocker before treating the run as RED. An expected exception may be the behavior under test; it is not automatically a setup error.

If the test passes immediately, determine whether it covers existing behavior, misses the intended defect, or exposes a mistaken requirement. Do not alter valid behavior merely to manufacture a failure. Record the actual outcome and resolve the test or contract before proceeding.

## GREEN

Return the failing scenario and observed evidence to the active implementation workflow (**sdd-implement** or **sdd-steer**) for the smallest production change that satisfies the accepted contract. Run the focused test again and the relevant regression checks. If the test still fails, return the failure for repair. Do not weaken a valid assertion to make the implementation pass; correct an erroneous expectation only against independent contract evidence.

Report every observed failure and significant warning. Distinguish new failures, established baseline failures, and environment problems where evidence permits; an unexplained failure remains unresolved. A focused green run does not establish that the whole suite passes.

## REFACTOR and repeat

Improve test clarity and remove test duplication while preserving coverage. Return production-refactoring needs to the active implementation workflow within the accepted task scope. Re-run affected checks after changes; refactoring does not introduce new behavior. Repeat the cycle for remaining scenarios.

Return command and outcome evidence to **sdd-verify** and the active implementation workflow for the required boundary verification, including the declared full suite when project policy or the selected boundary requires it. Do not mark task completion from this development cycle alone.

## Interrupted or non-test-first work

When useful and safe, demonstrate regression-test sensitivity against a prior implementation in an isolated worktree or controlled fixture. # Writing good tests

Load this reference whenever writing or changing tests, introducing doubles, or adding test helpers. Each test should protect an observable contract and have a clear explanation of the defect it catches.

## Independent expectations and meaningful failures

- Before writing a test, identify a plausible incorrect branch, argument, result, state transition, or missing effect that it should detect.
- Derive expected values independently: use accepted contracts, literal outcomes, or hand-checked fixtures. Do not call the tested helper to compute both actual and expected values.
- Test outcomes and contract-relevant effects rather than private structure, arbitrary constants, or source-text presence. Exact wording or representation belongs in assertions when the accepted contract requires it.
- Exercise scripts with controlled inputs and inspect outputs, effects, and exit status. Evaluate agent instructions through the consuming agent's behavior; text-presence checks alone cannot demonstrate that a skill works. Structural validators remain useful for format constraints.
- Cover the boundary your code owns. Avoid retesting a dependency's documented internals or trivial forwarding unless your component adds validation, normalization, defaults, lifecycle obligations, or other consequential behavior.

## Real behavior and doubles

Prefer real components and simple controlled fixtures where practical. Use a double when isolation of an external, nondeterministic, costly, or otherwise unsuitable dependency is necessary for the scenario.

| Before introducing a double | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Replacement boundary | Understand the real operation's side effects and preserve those the scenario relies on. Replace the narrow dependency that needs isolation. |
| Returned data | Model realistic contract-compatible structures, including fields relevant to consumers and representative success and failure variants. |
| Assertions | Assert the component's resulting behavior. Argument, order, or call-count checks are appropriate when the interaction itself is part of its contract. |
| Setup complexity | Consider an integration test with real components if the double obscures the behavior or requires extensive imitation of the dependency. |
| Cleanup and helpers | Keep test-only cleanup and helper code in test utilities; do not add production methods solely for tests. Respect actual resource ownership. |

A double's existence or programmed answer is not evidence that the real component works. Ensure that an incorrect production path cannot satisfy the same assertions through a permissive fixture.

## Review sensitivity

Inspect whether plausible faults would fail the tests: for example, a wrong argument, skipped effect, incorrect branch, missing validation, or empty result. If such a fault survives, identify a coverage gap or a test that merely restates the implementation. Use an isolated mutation or controlled faulty fixture when needed to demonstrate sensitivity; do not damage the working code or require mutation tooling by default.

Prefer clear scenario names, narrow assertions, maintainable fixtures, and tests that expose useful failures. Split unrelated behaviors while keeping assertions together when they jointly establish one contract. Re-run changed tests and relevant regressions, and report the evidence and any unresolved gap.

## Examples

These are illustrative Python assertions; replace names and values with the current project's contracts.

```python

# Reusing the tested formatter on both sides cannot expose its defect.
```

# TextStats system specification

## Scope and authority

TextStats provides predictable line and word counts through a silent Python API and module-entry CLI. The accepted [PROJECT](PROJECT.md), [ARCHITECTURE](ARCHITECTURE.md) and [DECOMPOSITION](DECOMPOSITION.md) govern product purpose and structural boundaries. Python 3.11+, standard-library runtime and unittest are required. No implementation exists.

R-001 through R-013 specify the intended initial two-phase system; milestone labels identify delivery obligations without authorizing implementation. F-001 through F-004 retain the later separately requested range feature's contract as a deferred compatibility constraint. That feature is outside the initial executable hierarchy. No focused specification children are needed.

## Public API and values

### R-001 Direct exports and statistics

Importable `textstats` directly exports `TextStats`, `count_text` and `count_file`. `TextStats(lines: int, words: int)` is immutable, with integer, nonnegative fields and value equality. Construction with a negative count raises ValueError; a non-integer count raises TypeError. Boolean values are excluded from the count domain despite Python's bool/int subtype relationship. Invalid construction cannot create a value with an invalid field. Exception wording is not prescribed. These construction details settle the design's previously delegated integer-domain boundary.

### R-002 Whole-input counting API

The signatures are `count_text(text: str, *, strip_bom: bool = True) -> TextStats` and `count_file(path: str | os.PathLike[str], *, strip_bom: bool = True) -> TextStats`. The keyword-only policy has the same meaning for both. Both return whole-input counts, are silent on stdout/stderr, and expose no range parameter. Valid text/file calls with identical decoded contents and policy return equal values. Behavior for arguments outside the annotated input domains is not otherwise prescribed.

### R-003 Line semantics

CRLF is one terminator; lone CR and lone LF are terminators. Each terminator contributes one line. A nonempty final unterminated segment contributes one line. Empty text contributes zero lines, and a trailing terminator creates no additional phantom line. Other Unicode separators, including U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029, do not terminate lines. Apply R-005 before deciding whether a final segment is nonempty.

### R-004 Word semantics

The word count equals the number of elements produced by Python `str.split()` with no separator argument on the counted text. Unicode whitespace separates words and runs of whitespace add no empty words. Word semantics do not broaden line-terminator semantics.

### R-005 BOM policy

With `strip_bom=True`, remove exactly one leading U+FEFF from the complete text. Preserve a second leading BOM and every interior BOM. With `strip_bom=False`, preserve all BOMs. Retained BOM is ordinary non-whitespace, including in otherwise empty content. CLI `--keep-bom` selects the retaining policy. No other text normalization or rewriting is permitted.

### R-006 Named-file decode, failure and ownership

Read complete input as bytes and decode strict UTF-8, retaining newline characters exactly. A named-file API call raises the applicable OSError subclass for missing/unreadable files or read failures and UnicodeDecodeError for invalid UTF-8. Do not return a partial result. Close every handle opened by the utility on success and failure. Inputs remain byte-for-byte unchanged. No fallback encoding, replacement character or locale-dependent decode is permitted.

## CLI contracts

### R-007 Baseline named-file invocation

Phase 1 milestone 1.1 supplies `python -m textstats [--keep-bom] INPUT` with exactly one named-file input. Support `--` to terminate option processing so dash-prefixed filenames are usable. A literal filename `-` is a named-file input before milestone 2.2; after stdin delivery it denotes stdin, and an actual file with that name can be addressed as `./-`. Recognized options can precede or follow the input, subject to `--` termination. Do not interpret options appearing after `--` as options.

Success returns status 0, stdout exactly `lines=<N> words=<N>\n` using nonnegative decimal integers, and empty stderr. This remains the default format in phase 2. # Working branches and explicit integration

Use this protocol for a bounded implementation range, feature campaign, steering amendment, project preparation baseline, or selected document integration. **sdd-manage** establishes and coordinates the Git lifecycle; the active owner performs its scoped work and persistence. A direct invocation of a focused skill follows this same protocol. Read-only requests do not create branches or merge.

## Publish each commit

After **each workflow-owned commit**, push it to the established remote branch and verify remote containment before advancing project work or creating another commit. Do not accumulate local commits for later publication, including in an agent's temporary sandbox. This rule applies to preparation, reviews/revisions, maintenance, implementation, steering, feature incorporation, report-only commits and merge commits, including direct focused calls. The commit owner publishes; a coordinator/reviewer handoff must finish publication before the next work unit, whether independent or dependent.

Resolve eligible outstanding workflow commits before new commit-producing work. If publication fails, is uncertain or lacks an established destination, preserve the commit, reconcile the remote/recover access where supported, and report the pending operation. Pause workflow advancement and further commits until publication is verified. Commit inspection, push/readback and scoped recovery remain allowed to finish that operation. Do not switch branches, tools or workflows to accumulate unpublished work or evade a blocker.

An **explicit user instruction** for local-only work or deferred publication overrides this cadence only within its stated scope; report committed-but-unpushed state accurately. This rule does not authorize publication outside the granted scope, bypass host/repository restrictions, guess a destination or permit force-pushing. Per-commit pushes do not require per-commit merges or alter human acceptance and integration gates.

## Establish the working branch

Use [branch management](branch-management.md) for identities, targets, convention names, eligible creation/reuse, worktree preservation, and phase transitions. This document-only boundary does not require implementation phase completion. Otherwise push completed work and pause without merging. ## Merge, verify, and publish

1. Refresh the target from its established remote and inspect divergence and worktree state without discarding changes. Resolve non-fast-forward local/remote history through project policy, not force-push. Use a clean integration worktree if unrelated work prevents safe integration. Pin the verified working tip and refreshed target tip.
2. Check whether the working tip is already an ancestor of the target. If already integrated, inspect the existing merge/evidence and publication state; do not fabricate another merge or claim a new boundary. If a prior merge is awaiting publication, verify that state and finish its push.
3. Merge the pinned working tip into the target with `git merge --no-ff --no-commit <working-tip>`. Never substitute a fast-forward, squash, or rebase for the required two-parent boundary. Inspect conflicts and the full prospective result; preserve the merge state when blocked. Do not publish a conflicted or unverified result.
4. Use **sdd-verify** to assess the merged state and relevant target regressions. Resolve conflicts and defects only within the authorized boundary; an out-of-scope consequence needs a decision. 6. Push the target merge commit to its established remote branch and verify containment. A task-branch push or local merge alone does not establish published integration. 7. Report working/target branches, task/amendment commits, merge SHA, verification, publication, and remaining differences. ## Continue a blocked workflow

## Platform authorization rejection

For a host denial, retain the commit, attempted destination/ref and actual reason. Distinguish denial from missing credentials; use available scope/evidence only through a supported resolution, without inventing an approval mechanism or asking for a grant already present. Inspect the remote first if the effect is uncertain. Do not repeat an unchanged denied operation, substitute credentials for a policy restriction, or switch tools/transports/accounts to evade it. ## Push authentication recovery

For a 403 or explicit missing/invalid-credential failure, use [hosting credentials and shell recovery](credentials.md), passing sanitized destination, operation, transport, and cause. Recover the current client's access and retry the same established destination; classify rate-limit or policy restrictions before replacing a token. This includes initial document preparation or review records, not just the first implementation task. “Initial” means SDD adoption in an already eligible Git worktree; do not initialize Git implicitly. Read-only orientation, discussion, selection and verification create nothing.

**sdd-manage** owns this shared policy and coordinates bootstrap for preparation, maintenance and feature incorporation. **sdd-implement** and **sdd-steer** apply it in their own commit procedures, including direct invocations. **sdd-report** checks bootstrap evidence when composing a commit but does not write or commit files. Load this reference at greenfield entry and before the first persistence operation in other adoption workflows; it is an ordinary agent procedure, not a hidden hook or client installer.

For implementation, push outstanding commits first under the existing startup protocol, then perform bootstrap before staging the first new result. Do not make a separate bootstrap commit ahead of the requested result. A preparation-only request can bootstrap with its preparation commit and still stop before implementation.

## Root artifacts and discoverability

Ensure root AGENTS.md through [agent orientation](agent-orientation.md) during authorized adoption. Read existing controlling instructions first; preserve manual content and explicit path limits. Include affected orientation with the same first result checkpoint, not a separate administrative commit. Its ownership and subsequent maintenance are independent of disclosure byte-copy requirements.

Resolve assets relative to the loaded plugin root: this reference is at `skills/sdd-manage/references/repository-bootstrap.md`; bundled files are at `assets/AI_DISCLOSURE.md` and `assets/SDD-MANAGER.md`. Use the same installed or pinned source as the running skills, including an acceptance vendor snapshot. Do not fetch a newer template silently or fabricate a missing asset.

1. Inspect the target Git root, applicable instructions, root `AI_DISCLOSURE.md`, `SDD-MANAGER.md`, README and relevant Git history. Establish bootstrap ownership separately from unrelated pending content. For a project nested in a Git repository, place these records at the **target repository root**, not inside `docs/dev/` or the project subdirectory; resolve incompatible repository-wide scope before writing.
2. If absent, copy `assets/AI_DISCLOSURE.md` byte for byte to root `AI_DISCLOSURE.md` and `assets/SDD-MANAGER.md` to root `SDD-MANAGER.md`. The notice names SDD Manager and links `https://github.com/pchemguy/SDD-Manager`; it links the root disclosure and makes no unsupported completion claim. Never include credentials or local installation paths.
3. Add a concise discoverable root README link, preserving its project focus and existing text:

   `Development uses [SDD Manager](SDD-MANAGER.md). See the [AI-assisted development disclosure](AI_DISCLOSURE.md).`

   Reuse an existing equivalent link instead of duplicating it. If no root README exists, create a minimal `README.md` with the established project name and these links; do not invent product claims. Where the repository uses another designated root README, use that document and correct relative links.
4. Preserve existing disclosures and usage notices. If byte-identical, reuse them. If different, read and reconcile within authorized scope: retain project-specific disclosure and truthful attribution, add the required SDD Manager link, and do not replace established text with a template. Conflicting disclosure claims or ownership require a decision before the affected commit. Do not follow a symlink to edit an external file or directory.
5. Inspect links, truthful scope, file ownership and the staged diff. Include the owned root changes with the first verified SDD result and its ordinary status/evidence changes; apply the existing unrelated-index isolation, commit and push/readback rules. Verify the committed tree contains the required root records and README links, and an added disclosure matches its packaged bytes. A draft or untracked copy is not completion.

## Scope limits, recovery and upgrades

These files are ordinary bootstrap outputs of an authorized initial SDD workflow. Explicit human restrictions such as selected-path-only, no README edits, or read-only take precedence. If those restrictions exclude a required missing artifact, report the bootstrap scope conflict and obtain the missing decision rather than silently widening paths or falsely claiming bootstrap complete. Honor local-only/no-push instructions; bootstrap itself does not authorize publication.

On interruption, inspect actual files, index and Git evidence. Reuse valid pending copies in the same first result, preserving unrelated staged work. If the first SDD commit already includes the records, continue its pending push instead of making another bootstrap commit. On subsequent invocations, retain established files and links without duplicate sections or version churn. If an older SDD-managed repository lacks the records, add them to the next authorized coherent commit within scope and report this as adoption backfill; never rewrite history or claim they were in its original first commit. Report missing/conflicting records for scoped repair when their creation is not currently authorized.

A plugin update does not automatically overwrite the target's disclosure or notice. Version/commit provenance may be added when accurately known, but is not a prerequisite and must not misrepresent a dirty-source snapshot as a released version.

## Human review at startup

Apply [human document review](human-document-review.md) from greenfield entry. Walk the human through necessary new documents, pausing at each created root before dependent work. For existing or interrupted main/feature preparation, assess progress and reuse acceptable inputs without automatically entering interactive mode. Begin with explicitly requested interactive reviews; raise important startup concerns and offer review before advancing. Retain real pending review/stopping instructions.

Task-associated subjects must begin with exactly one owning `[<task-id>]` marker and an imperative description; use the [task subject rules](references/object-drafts.md#task-commit-subjects) and return composition conflicts to the commit owner. This skill drafts reports and messages. The active implementation or steering workflow owns its work commits and task status; **sdd-manage** coordinates other persistence and explicit boundary merges, **sdd-forge** owns hosted issue/milestone mutations, and any future PR workflow owns PR creation or merge. A draft does not grant authorization for those actions or establish task completion. Return the draft, source task IDs and issue references actually resolved, evidence used, and any facts still needed before publication.
# Issue, commit, and PR drafts

Keep the same task identity across all outputs. Use the project-wide ID from its owning TASKS or FEATURE-TASKS entry; include a resolved issue reference only when **sdd-forge** supplies a unique repository and number. Match the requested object's time perspective: an issue describes intended work, while a commit or PR describes actual changes and available evidence.

## Task issue

Return `title` and `body` separately. Format the title as `[<task-id>] <task title>`, using the owning task list. Draft the body from the task outcome, reason and project context, expected scope and dependencies, objective acceptance and prescribed checks, and source document links. Add relevant kind-specific details. For example:

- **Performance:** Describe the problem with the current implementation, explain how the proposed approach may improve it, and identify the measurement plan and any established baseline. Do not present an expected speedup as an achieved result.
- **Security:** State the affected guarantee and risk without exposing exploit instructions or credentials.

**sdd-report** owns the title and body format. Preserve an exact task identity marker when one is supplied. Never invent host labels, milestone associations, issue URLs, or resolution state.

## Git commit

For a first SDD commit or adoption backfill, load **sdd-manage**'s [repository bootstrap](../../sdd-manage/references/repository-bootstrap.md). Confirm the commit owner has included or validly retained root disclosure/usage records and README links within scope. Return missing bootstrap evidence to that owner; drafting does not perform bootstrap or establish a committed result.

Draft a short imperative subject naming the actual change, based on the inspected diff and checks rather than merely the task brief. Use a body when the reason, verification, migration implications or verified issue references need explanation.

### Task commit subjects

For every task-associated commit, use exactly `[<owning-task-id>] <imperative description>`. The single owning task marker must be the first content of the subject, followed by one space and the description. Preserve the exact project-wide ID from TASKS or FEATURE-TASKS. Do not prepend a conventional-commit type/scope, put the ID only at the end, or use multiple task IDs or a task range in the subject. Apply this format to production, tests, documentation and explicit milestone/phase review/report tasks, as well as authorized partial checkpoints and later task-specific repairs or parent-status follow-ups. Describe partial or follow-up work accurately; a subject does not establish completion.

For numeric `T-` IDs padded to at least three digits, `^\[T-[0-9]{3,}\] [^\r\n]+$` checks the basic subject shape. Also check that the ID is the exact owning entry, the subject has no second task identity, and the description is concise, imperative and truthful. A regex alone cannot establish ownership, single-task composition or completion.

| Subject | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| `[T-028] Implement lock delay` | Valid shape for one verified owning task. |
| `[T-030] Complete Milestone 2.4 review` | Valid for the review task's actual result and completion. |
| `[T-028] Record partial lock-delay checkpoint` | Valid shape; retain unchecked status and required checkpoint authority. |
| `feat(mechanics): [T-028] Implement lock delay` | Invalid: content precedes the task marker. |
| `Implement lock delay (T-028)` | Invalid: task marker is not at the beginning. |
| `[T-028, T-029] Implement lock delay and wall kicks` | Invalid: multiple owning tasks. |
| `[T-028] Implement lock delay and close T-029` | Invalid: second task identity, despite passing the shape regex. |

- **Review:** Actual reviewed scope/coverage and material conclusions; state when no separate review was performed. Do not imply a comprehensive review from a focused amendment.
- **Delivered:** Actual executed scope and consequential features/fixes/documentation or workflow changes, including effects relevant to users. Separate accepted/executed work from proposals, exclusions and unfinished parent work.
- **Verification:** Actual boundary and merged-state checks/results, with relevant counts/environment and evidence limits. Retain relevant earlier information without copying raw prior messages or presenting original delivery as new. Correct superseded outcomes in the cumulative result and distinguish historical checks/source from actual new merged-state verification; inherited verification is not fresh evidence.

Carry needed scope distinctions forward in the latest message rather than requiring readers to follow older merge bodies; distinguish these provenance references from the cumulative user outcome and current delta. They are not a new registry or raw chronological transcript.

The campaign-opening commit is the verified first commit opening that campaign and its retained records. It is distinct from the branch-off/shared source checkpoint and from later reopening commits; do not infer it from current branch tips or invent an unavailable identity.

An enclosing integration summarizes the combined delivered result and identifies included nested campaigns/amendments sufficiently to prevent duplicate release highlights. Keep the semantic summary prominent and technical provenance compact; do not substitute raw logs or a list of commit subjects for the outcome.

Phase summaries describe actual completed phase scope, delivery/reviews/exits and verification; retain the full-phase merge gate and report an explicit partial-integration override accurately. Document-preparation summaries identify accepted documents/review coverage and readiness for their dependent stage, without claiming implementation or task completion. Use the plugin’s established `design-docs/*` document-preparation branches; prefixes discover candidates but never establish scope or acceptance. Preserve repeated preparation deltas as distinct scope, with appropriate source/checkpoint evidence.

The message is an **integration summary**, not proof that closure/publication already happened. It is committed before its push and final worktree return; do not claim those future steps succeeded. Draft a title and description only when requested; this skill does not create a PR. Scope the text to the actual branch diff and its included task IDs. # Inspection and handoff

Use this reference for read-only orientation. Collect enough evidence for the contemplated action; do not dump an entire monorepo into context.

## Project and authority

- Resolve the user-supplied path or current directory to a project root. In a monorepo, distinguish the governed subproject from the containing repository. When candidates are genuinely ambiguous, report them instead of choosing one silently.
- Read applicable root and more deeply scoped `AGENTS.md` files for anticipated paths. Follow their relevant references and project-designated instruction sources, including policies outside the project root when they apply.
- Identify contradictory or unreadable instructions and the exact affected action. Record rules for language, build, test, documentation, generated files, source ownership, and commit practices when relevant.
- Inspect `docs/dev/PROJECT.md` as the project brief. Determine the role of its actual contents. If it contains operating instructions, report them as applicable instructions and identify their scope and any conflict; document revision is a separate workflow.

## Git evidence

Use Git's inspection commands with optional writes suppressed. Plain `git status` can refresh index metadata even when file contents are unchanged. Apply `git --no-optional-locks` to each inspection command, or scope `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` to the inspection process; do not change repository or global configuration. For example, from the candidate project path:

```text
git --no-optional-locks rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree
git --no-optional-locks rev-parse --show-toplevel
git --no-optional-locks symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD
git --no-optional-locks rev-parse --verify HEAD
git --no-optional-locks status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all
```

Distinguish a Git worktree from a bare repository, a Git directory outside the target project, or a path with no Git. Record branch or detached state; record an unborn HEAD explicitly. Note staged, unstaged, untracked, deleted, renamed, conflicted, and submodule changes where present. Scope status to the project and anticipated target paths without concealing relevant parent-level or shared files.

Do not assume dirty paths belong to the current task or the agent. Do not interpret clean status alone as proof that the intended work is finished or that documents agree.
